weeks.title: Environmental Concerns, Population Growth and Resource Consumption
atAGlance: Contaminant = present; pollutant = present + harm (concentration + toxicity + exposure).
Population models: arithmetic P0+nX; geometric P0(1+r)^n; exponential P0 e^(rn). Same r → arithmetic < geometric < exponential.
IPAT: I = P × A × T. Impact scales with population, affluence, and technology intensity.
EF demand vs biocapacity supply; both in global hectares (gha). World EF ~2.8 gha/cap vs BC ~1.6 gha/cap.
Earth Overshoot Day: date when annual demand exceeds Earth’s yearly biocapacity.
EPI (Energy Performance Index) = annual energy / floor area (kWh/m²·y); LCA tracks cradle-to-grave burdens.
Petropolis = fossil-fuel-dependent city; urban metabolism = city as organism of energy/material flows.

definitions.definition: Any substance present in air, water, or soil that is not normally there, or present above background levels.
definitions.trap: Presence alone ≠ pollution. Without demonstrated adverse effect it remains a contaminant.

definitions.definition: A contaminant that causes adverse effects on humans, biota, or materials at the concentration and exposure of interest.
Benefit humans derive from ecosystems (provisioning, regulating, supporting, cultural) without engineered substitutes.
Regenerative capacity of ecosystems to produce useful biological materials and absorb wastes, expressed in global hectares (gha).
definitions.trap: Biocapacity is supply; Ecological Footprint is demand. Do not swap them.

definitions.definition: Hectare of land with world-average biological productivity. Used to compare unlike land types via equivalence factors (EQF).
Biologically productive area required to produce the resources a population consumes and to absorb its wastes (esp. CO₂), in gha.
Calendar date when humanity’s cumulative EF since 1 Jan exceeds Earth’s biocapacity for that year.
Building energy intensity: annual energy use divided by floor area, typically kWh/m²·year.
I = P × A × T: Environmental Impact = Population × Affluence × Technology (impact intensity).
Urban form whose metabolism depends heavily on fossil fuels for transport, buildings, and goods — opposite of a solar/circular city framing.

blocks.text: Environment spans atmosphere, hydrosphere, lithosphere, and biosphere. Course framing links pollution control, climate, waste, water, soil, and public health under one sustainability lens.

items: Air: industrial and vehicular emissions, stubble/waste burning, Urban Heat Island (UHI), climate change.
Water: scarcity of safe drinking water, wastewater loads on aquatic ecosystems.
Soil: salinization, erosion, nutrient depletion, synthetic organics.
Biodiversity: extinction, bioaccumulation of toxics.

blocks.text: Exam favourite: contaminant vs pollutant. Contaminant = presence; pollutant = presence + adverse effect. Always cite concentration, toxicity, and exposure pathway.
UHI: urban surfaces (asphalt, concrete) store and re-radiate heat; nights stay warmer than rural surrounds. Stubble burning spikes North Indian PM in Oct–Nov.
Do not say ‘all contaminants are pollutants’. Arsenic in groundwater can be natural yet still a pollutant if it harms health.

items: Natural sources: volcanoes, forest fires, dust storms.
Anthropogenic: vehicles, power plants, industry, biomass/waste burning.
Of ~30 most polluted cities globally, a large share is routinely in India (course slide claim — know the framing).

blocks.text: Brundtland (Our Common Future, 1987): development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.

items: Three pillars: environment, economy, society (equity across time and within generations).
Natural services cannot be fully substituted by technology at planetary scale.
Course objective: embed SD in daily decisions; Supreme Court M.C. Mehta vs Union of India (1991) pushed environmental education.

blocks.text: Week 2 expands Brundtland into planetary boundaries, MDGs/SDGs, and the 5 Ps. Memorize the verbatim definition here first.
Resource consumption and pollution rise with population and with per-capita intensity. Quantification tools in this week: population models, IPAT, EF, Overshoot Day, EPI, LCA.
Three classic discrete/continuous models appear in numerical questions. Always identify whether growth is fixed increment (arithmetic) or rate-based (geometric/exponential).

blocks.title: Arithmetic vs geometric vs exponential (P0=1000, r=0.1 or X=100, n=10)

blocks.use: Arithmetic: planned/fixed headcount increase; X = absolute increment per period.
Geometric: percentage growth compounded once per period (census-style discrete steps).
Exponential: continuous growth; for same r and n, largest of the three.

blocks.text: Order for identical P0, r, n: arithmetic < geometric < exponential. Drill 1000 / 0.1 / 10 → 2000, 2594, 2718.
Goodness of fit: R² near 1 means the model explains almost all variance in the series. India census series often fit exponential with high R² in course examples.

items: R² → 1: strong fit; model useful for short-term projection.
R² low: wrong model form, structural breaks, or policy shocks.
Carrying capacity / logistic growth appears later (Week 11 ecology); Week 1 sticks to unlimited J-curve forms.

blocks.text: Using r=10% as 10 instead of 0.1 in e^(rn) is a common arithmetic error. Keep r as a fraction.

blocks.use: Impact = Population × Affluence (consumption/cap) × Technology (impact per unit consumption).

blocks.text: Example framing for CO₂: I ≈ population × (fossil kWh/cap·y) × (kg CO₂/kWh). Cutting T (cleaner tech) can offset rising P and A, but only if T falls faster than P×A grows.

items: P: population size and growth rate.
A: GDP/cap or energy/cap — lifestyle and wealth.
T: emission factor, material intensity, efficiency of conversion.

blocks.text: When factors multiply, approximate % changes add. If P +2%, A +3%, T −4%, net I ≈ +1%.
IPAT is a decomposition identity, not a full causal model. Do not claim it ‘proves’ one driver alone.

sections.title: Ecological Footprint and Earth Overshoot Day

blocks.text: EF converts consumption into land/sea area needed. Biocapacity is what ecosystems can regenerate. Units: global hectares (gha).

blocks.use: Production P (t/y) scaled by world-average yield Y_w and equivalence factor EQF → gha.
National area An, national/world yield ratio, EQF — supply side of the ledger.

items: EF components often include cropland, grazing, forest, fishing, built-up, carbon footprint.
Deficit mechanisms: net-import biocapacity; overharvest domestic stock; emit more CO₂ than sinks absorb.
Global: ~2.8 gha/person demand vs ~1.6 gha/person biocapacity → structural overshoot.

blocks.text: Overshoot Day later in the year = less overshoot that year. 2020 delayed because lockdown cut demand, not because biocapacity magically rose.
EF is not GDP. A rich efficient country can have lower EF/cap than a poorer high-biomass consumer — compare carefully.

blocks.use: kWh (or MJ) per year per m² of floor area; compare buildings and campuses.

items: Use 3–5 years of utility bills for a stable EPI.
Lower EPI → better energy performance for similar climate/use.
LCA (Life Cycle Assessment): inventory + impact from cradle to grave (or cradle to cradle).

blocks.text: Urban metabolism treats the city as an organism: inputs (energy, water, food, materials), stocks (buildings, infrastructure), outputs (waste, emissions, heat). Petropolis = high fossil throughput.

items: Map flows (energy, water, materials, waste).
Normalize by population or floor area (links to EPI).
Identify leverage: efficiency, fuel switch, circular loops.
Compare to biocapacity / EF narrative at city scale.

blocks.text: EPI example pattern: sum annual kWh from bills ÷ built-up m². Units must be kWh/m²·y (or consistent energy unit).
Links forward to Week 5 renewable supply and Week 7 industrial ecology / circular economy.

Air quality concerns (PM, UHI context) deepen into pollutant physics and control.
Carbon footprint in EF connects to GHG accounting and climate treaties.
Cutting T in IPAT via renewables — solar/wind replace fossil intensity.

weeks.title: Principles of Sustainable Development
atAGlance: Brundtland 1987 verbatim: meet present needs without compromising future generations’ ability to meet theirs.
Timeline: Silent Spring (1962) → Stockholm (1972) → Brundtland (1987) → Rio (1992) → MDGs (2000) → SDGs (2015).
Nine planetary boundaries; crossed (course): biodiversity loss, climate change, N cycle, land-system change.
MDGs: 8 goals, developing focus; SDGs: 17 goals, universal, leave no one behind.
5 Ps: People, Planet, Prosperity, Peace, Partnership.
SDG Index ranks countries on progress; watch negative spillover (exports of harm).
Extensive green roof and Smart City as urban SD interventions.

definitions.definition: Development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.
definitions.trap: Learn the sentence verbatim — MCQs often tweak one clause.

definitions.definition: Safe operating space for humanity across nine Earth-system processes; crossing raises risk of abrupt/irreversible change.
Proposed epoch in which human activity is the dominant driver of planetary change.
Millennium Development Goals (2000–2015): eight goals mainly aimed at developing countries’ poverty and basic needs.
Sustainable Development Goals (Agenda 2030): 17 goals, 169 targets, universal to all countries.
People, Planet, Prosperity, Peace, Partnership — framing pillars of the 2030 Agenda.
Composite score/rank of countries’ progress toward the SDGs (e.g. SDSN reports).
When a country’s consumption or production imposes environmental/social costs outside its borders (e.g. imported deforestation).
Lightweight vegetated roof with thin substrate; stormwater, insulation, biodiversity benefits at lower load than intensive gardens.
ICT-enabled urban management aiming at efficiency, livability, and sustainability (India Smart Cities Mission as course context).

blocks.text: UN Brundtland Commission (1983), chaired by Gro Harlem Brundtland. Report: Our Common Future (1987). Canonical SD definition is examined verbatim.
Write exactly: ‘Development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.’

items: Environment: stay within ecological limits / planetary boundaries.
Economy: livelihoods and growth that do not liquidate natural capital.
Society: intra- and inter-generational equity.
Needs of the poor often get priority language in Brundtland framing.

blocks.text: SD ≠ ‘green growth’ slogan alone. If future options shrink, it fails the Brundtland test even if GDP rises.

sections.title: From Silent Spring to SDGs — timeline

blocks.title: Milestone timeline
rows: First major global environment conference; UNEP born

blocks.text: Order drill: Silent Spring → Stockholm → Brundtland → Rio → MDGs → SDGs. Pair Rio 1992 with UNFCCC (Week 4).

items: Awareness literature and local pollution crises.
International soft law and institutions (UNEP).
SD concept formalized (1987).
Harder treaty architecture (1992+).
Development goals (MDGs then universal SDGs).

blocks.text: Rockström et al. framework: nine boundaries defining a safe operating space. Course stresses which have been crossed.

items: Climate change
Biosphere integrity (biodiversity loss)
Biogeochemical flows (N and P cycles)
Land-system change
Freshwater use
Ocean acidification
Atmospheric aerosol loading
Stratospheric ozone depletion
Novel entities (chemical pollution)

blocks.text: Crossed (course emphasis): biodiversity loss, climate change, nitrogen cycle, land-system change. Ozone is a recovery success story (links Montreal, Week 3).
‘Nine boundaries’ ≠ ‘nine already crossed’. Know the list and the crossed subset separately.
Anthropocene framing: human forcing rivals geologic drivers. SD policy = keep humanity inside the safe space while meeting needs.

sections.title: MDGs vs SDGs and the 5 Ps

items: People — dignity, equality, healthy lives.
Planet — protect ecosystems for present and future.
Prosperity — progress in harmony with nature.
Peace — just, inclusive societies.
Partnership — Global Partnership for Sustainable Development.

blocks.text: 5 Ps mnemonic: People, Planet, Prosperity, Peace, Partnership. MDG→SDG = from 8/developing to 17/universal.
SDG Index scores countries on goal progress. High domestic scores can hide negative spillover: pollution, land use, or labour impacts exported via trade.
Negative spillover = harm abroad from domestic consumption patterns. Exam may contrast rank vs responsibility.

items: Extensive green roof: thin growing medium, low structural load; reduces runoff, cools roof, adds habitat.
Intensive green roof: deeper soil, trees/gardens — heavier, more amenity, higher cost.
Smart City: sensors, data, e-governance for mobility, energy, water, waste — SD only if equity and environment are designed in.

blocks.text: Smart ≠ automatically sustainable. ICT without demand reduction can raise energy use (rebound).
Week 1 EF/overshoot = biophysical budget; Week 2 SDGs = governance targets on that budget.

Course/SDSN-style transformations group SDGs into actionable clusters (education, health, energy decarbonization, sustainable food, cities, digital). Trade-offs are normal: biofuel land vs food (Week 6), densification vs green space.

items: Set measurable targets (SDG indicators).
Stay within planetary boundaries (biophysical).
Finance and partnership (5th P).
Monitor spillovers, not only domestic KPIs.
Iterate policy with science–policy bodies (IPCC link in Week 4).

blocks.text: Be ready to map one local intervention (green roof / Smart City measure) to at least two SDGs (e.g. 11 cities, 13 climate).

crossLinks.why: Brundtland sentence and EF/biocapacity are the biophysical side of SD.
Ozone boundary recovery via Montreal shows governance success.
Rio 1992 → UNFCCC; climate boundary is SDG 13 core.
Energy access and decarbonization sit inside SDG 7 and SEE trilemma.

examChecklist: Recite Brundtland definition word-perfect.
Order Silent Spring → Stockholm → Brundtland → Rio → MDGs → SDGs with years.
List 9 planetary boundaries; name crossed ones.
Fill MDG vs SDG comparison table from memory.
Name the 5 Ps.
Define negative spillover with one trade example.
Extensive vs intensive green roof in one line each.
One Smart City benefit + one rebound risk.

weeks.title: Understanding Air Pollution
atAGlance: Ambient air = outdoor air in the troposphere that we breathe in the open environment.
Primary = emitted as-is; secondary = formed in atmosphere (e.g. O₃, some aerosols).
Criteria pollutants regulated for ambient standards; hazardous air pollutants (HAPs) are toxics at low dose.
DALR ≈ 9.8 °C/km; compare to ELR to judge stability / inversion.
PM0.1 (ultrafine) penetrates deepest into alveoli/bloodstream pathway framing.
Ground-level O₃ is secondary (NOx + VOC + sunlight); Montreal 1987 targets ODS.
NAQI = MAX of sub-indices; control: SCR → N₂+H₂O; FGD for SO₂; ESP 95–99%.
ASEAN Haze Agreement 2002 — transboundary smoke from land/forest fires.

definitions.definition: Outdoor air in the surrounding environment (troposphere) as distinct from indoor or workplace air.
Emitted directly from sources (e.g. SO₂, NO, CO, primary PM).
Formed by atmospheric reactions (e.g. O₃, secondary PM/sulfate/nitrate).
definitions.trap: O₃ at ground level is secondary; do not call stack O₃ a primary emission.

definitions.definition: Common pollutant with ambient air quality standards (typically SO₂, NO₂, CO, O₃, PM, Pb in many regimes).
Toxic pollutant harmful at low concentrations (carcinogens, etc.); regulated differently from criteria set.
Dry Adiabatic Lapse Rate ≈ 9.8 °C/km: cooling rate of a dry air parcel rising adiabatically.
Layer where temperature increases with height; suppresses vertical mixing and traps pollutants.
National Air Quality Index: overall index taken as the maximum of pollutant sub-indices for the period.
definitions.trap: NAQI is MAX, not average, of sub-indices.

definitions.definition: Ozone-Depleting Substances (CFCs, halons, etc.) controlled under the Montreal Protocol (1987).

blocks.text: Ambient air quality drives outdoor exposure. Indoor air pollution (cooking fuels, etc.) is a separate but linked health burden.

blocks.title: Primary vs secondary; criteria vs hazardous

items: Natural sources: volcanoes, dust, wildfires, biogenic VOCs.
Anthropogenic: combustion, industry, vehicles, agriculture, waste burning.
Size matters for PM: coarse vs fine vs ultrafine deposition depth.

blocks.text: PM0.1 (ultrafine) — deepest respiratory penetration in course framing. PM2.5 dominates health-burden discussion.

blocks.use: Dry parcel cooling with height; compare with environmental lapse rate (ELR).

blocks.text: Inversion: temperature rises with height in a layer. Nighttime radiation inversions and subsidence inversions both worsen urban smog episodes.
Stable atmosphere ≠ ‘good weather for air quality’. Stable/inversion = poor dispersion.
Memorize DALR ≈ 9.8 °C/km and the three comparison cases with ELR.

sections.title: Ozone: tropospheric smog vs stratospheric ODS

blocks.text: Tropospheric (ground-level) O₃: secondary pollutant from NOx + VOCs + sunlight. Respiratory irritant; criteria pollutant.
Stratospheric O₃: protective UV shield. ODS (CFCs, halons, etc.) catalytically destroy it. Montreal Protocol (1987) phases down ODS — major policy success.

items: Do not confuse ‘good up high, bad nearby’ ozone.
Montreal 1987 ≠ Kyoto/Paris (those are climate, Week 4).
Some ODS are also strong GHGs — dual benefit of phase-out.

blocks.text: O₃ is secondary. Montreal Protocol year = 1987. Link to planetary boundary recovery (Week 2).
Attributing ground-level O₃ solely to ‘ozone hole chemistry’ is wrong — different altitude, different problem.

blocks.use: Overall category follows the worst pollutant sub-index for the averaging period.

blocks.text: Sub-indices map concentrations to a common 0–500-style scale. Reporting the max avoids masking a spike in one pollutant by averaging with clean others.
If PM2.5 sub-index = 280 and others < 100, NAQI = 280. Not the mean.

items: Short-term: asthma attacks, hospital admissions.
Long-term: cardiopulmonary mortality, DALYs from ambient + household air pollution.
Children and elderly are sensitive subgroups.

blocks.title: Key end-of-pipe controls
rows: Reduces NOx to N₂ + H₂O with ammonia/urea + catalyst
Scrubs SO₂ from flue gas (wet/dry lime/limestone systems)
Fabric filtration; cyclones for coarser fractions

blocks.use: Remember products: nitrogen gas and water — not ‘filtered NOx sludge’ as the main story.

blocks.text: Match: SCR↔NOx; FGD↔SO₂; ESP↔PM at 95–99%. Primary prevention (fuel switch) still beats end-of-pipe alone.
ESP does not remove SO₂ or NOx gases. Wrong pairing loses easy marks.
ASEAN Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution (2002) addresses smoke from land and forest fires crossing borders in Southeast Asia.

items: Drivers: peat/forest clearing, dry season fires, agricultural burning.
Impacts: ambient PM spikes, health, aviation, tourism.
Governance lesson: airsheds ignore borders — needs regional law.

blocks.text: Compare with North India stubble burning (Week 1 concern) — similar PM pathway, different legal instrument.
ASEAN Haze Agreement year = 2002.

crossLinks.why: Major air concerns and UHI/stubble context introduced.
Ozone boundary and Montreal as SD governance success.
Some air pollutants/ODS overlap with GHG and climate policy.
Cleaner energy supply reduces primary combustion emissions.

examChecklist: Define ambient air; primary vs secondary with O₃ example.
Criteria vs HAP in one contrast sentence.
DALR value; three ELR comparison cases; define inversion.
PM0.1 deepest penetration.
NAQI = MAX sub-index — worked mini example.
SCR products N₂+H₂O; FGD for SO₂; ESP 95–99%.
Montreal 1987 ODS; ASEAN Haze 2002.
Good-up-high vs bad-nearby ozone one-liner.

weeks.title: Climate Change: Scientific Basis, Mitigation and Adaptation
atAGlance: Weather = short-term state; climate = long-term statistics, typically ≥30 years.
Key GHGs: CO₂, CH₄, N₂O, O₃ (tropospheric), fluorinated gases (CFCs/HFCs/etc.).
GWP(CO₂) = 1 by definition; compare others over a chosen time horizon (often 100 y).
CFCs are anthropogenic (no significant natural source) — strong ODS and GHG link.
Ice–albedo feedback: melt → lower albedo → more absorption → more melt.
UNFCCC 1992 → Kyoto 1997 (force 2005, Annex I −5.2%) → Paris 2015; CBDR principle.
IPCC assesses literature; does not produce original research. Peace Nobel 2007 (with Gore).
Mitigation = cut causes; adaptation = live with impacts; carbon credits trade verified reductions.

definitions.definition: Atmospheric conditions over short timescales (hours to days) at a place.
Long-term statistics of weather, conventionally described over periods of about 30 years or more.
definitions.trap: One hot week is weather, not proof of climate change by itself.

definitions.definition: Gas that absorbs/emits infrared radiation, warming the troposphere (enhanced greenhouse effect when concentrations rise).
Global Warming Potential: cumulative radiative forcing of a mass of gas relative to the same mass of CO₂ over a chosen time horizon.
Fraction of incident solar radiation reflected by a surface; ice/snow high, open ocean/forest lower.
United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (adopted 1992, Rio) — parent climate treaty.
Common But Differentiated Responsibilities — shared climate duty with different obligations by capacity/history.
Actions that reduce GHG emissions or enhance sinks.
Adjustments in systems to moderate harm or exploit opportunities from climate change.
Tradable certificate representing a verified reduction/removal of GHGs, typically 1 tCO₂e.

sections.title: Weather vs climate and the enhanced greenhouse effect

blocks.text: Climate change science starts by separating weather noise from climate signal. Standards use multi-decadal baselines (≥30 y).
Climate ≈ ≥30-year statistics. Quote this threshold in definitions.

items: Natural greenhouse effect keeps Earth habitable.
Enhanced effect: anthropogenic GHG rise → extra trapping of IR → warming.
Indicators: global mean temperature, sea level, ice mass, extremes frequency.

blocks.text: ‘Climate has always changed’ does not refute anthropogenic forcing rates in the instrumental era.

blocks.title: Major GHGs (course set)
rows: Dominant stock GHG from fossil fuels & land use

blocks.use: Reference; other gases reported as CO₂-equivalents via GWP × mass.

blocks.text: CFCs are anthropogenic — essentially no natural source. Dual role: ODS (Montreal) and GHG.
CO₂e accounting: multiply mass of each gas by its GWP and sum. Horizon choice (20 vs 100 y) changes CH₄’s apparent weight.

items: Warming melts ice/snow.
Surface albedo falls (darker ocean/land exposed).
More solar absorption.
Further warming — positive feedback.
Water vapour feedback: warmer air holds more H₂O (itself a GHG).
Cloud feedbacks: sign/magnitude more uncertain — exam: name uncertainty, don’t invent certainty.
Permafrost carbon: thaw can release CH₄/CO₂.

blocks.text: Ice–albedo = classic positive feedback. Draw the four-step loop in 30 seconds.

blocks.title: Treaty timeline
rows: Annex I aggregate target about −5.2% vs 1990 (commitment period framing)

blocks.text: Annex I: industrialized parties with quantified Kyoto targets. Non-Annex I: developing parties without the same Kyoto QELRCs. Paris shifts to nationally determined contributions for all parties.
Kyoto: 1997 adopt / 2005 force / Annex I ≈ 5.2% reduction. Paris: 2015. UNFCCC: 1992.
Montreal (ODS, 1987) is not a Kyoto substitute. Different problem, different treaty.

items: CBDR: common responsibility for the climate system; differentiated duties.
Equity and historical emissions inform differentiation debates.
Finance, technology transfer, capacity building are CBDR operational tools.

blocks.text: IPCC (Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change) assesses peer-reviewed science and produces Assessment Reports. It does not conduct original experimental research as its mandate.
IPCC = assessment body, not a primary research lab. Nobel Peace Prize 2007 awarded to IPCC and Al Gore.

items: Working groups cover physical science, impacts/adaptation, mitigation.
Uncertainty language is calibrated (likely, very likely, etc.).
Policy-relevant, not policy-prescriptive — informs negotiators.

blocks.text: Saying ‘IPCC invented climate models from scratch as new data’ misstates the assessment role.

blocks.title: Mitigation vs adaptation
rows: Sea walls, drought-resistant crops, early warning

blocks.text: Carbon credit numerical pattern: project baseline emissions − project emissions = reductions. Credits issued for verified tonnes CO₂e; one credit ↔ 1 tCO₂e in standard markets.

blocks.use: Additionality and MRV required; double-counting forbidden in good practice.

items: Establish baseline (what would happen without project).
Implement mitigation project; monitor emissions.
Verify reductions; issue credits.
Buyer retires credit against a claim / compliance obligation.

blocks.text: Both mitigation and adaptation are needed. Credits are mitigation finance tools — they do not replace adaptation.
Week 5–6 renewables = major mitigation pathway; Week 2 SDG 13 frames policy goals.

crossLinks.why: Carbon footprint inside EF; IPAT technology term for fossil intensity.
Rio 1992 and climate planetary boundary / SDG 13.
O₃ dual role; ODS/Montreal overlap with fluorinated GHGs.
Solar and wind as primary mitigation technologies.

examChecklist: Weather vs climate with ≥30 y.
List five GHG groups; GWP(CO₂)=1; CFCs anthropogenic.
Draw ice–albedo positive feedback.
Define CBDR.
IPCC does not do original research; Nobel 2007.
Mitigation vs adaptation table.
Carbon credit = verified 1 tCO₂e pattern (baseline − project).

weeks.title: Renewable Energy I (Solar and Wind Energy)
atAGlance: RE: energy from resources that replenish on human timescales (solar, wind, hydro, geothermal, ocean, bio).
SEE trilemma: Security, Equity (access/affordability), Environmental sustainability — balance all three.
Betz limit: max Cp = 16/27 ≈ 59.3%; P_max = (8/27) ρ A v³.
Power in wind P = ½ ρ A v³; power scales with v³ — site wind speed dominates.
Trombe wall: passive solar heating via glazed thermal mass wall.
PV = photovoltaic electricity; CSP = concentrated solar thermal → heat/steam/power.
Active solar uses pumps/fans/controls; passive uses design/orientation/materials.
Capacity factor = actual energy / (rated power × time); technical potential = resource that is usable with tech constraints.

definitions.definition: Energy derived from natural processes that are replenished continuously or on short timescales relative to use.
Energy policy triangle: Security of supply, Equity (access/affordability), Environmental sustainability.
Theoretical maximum power coefficient for a wind turbine in open flow: Cp,max = 16/27.
definitions.trap: Real turbines are below Betz; Betz is an upper bound, not a typical operating point.

definitions.definition: Passive solar system: dark high-mass wall behind glazing absorbs sun and releases heat to the interior with time lag.
Direct conversion of sunlight to electricity via semiconductor cells/modules.
Concentrating Solar Power: mirrors/lenses concentrate sunlight to heat a fluid for thermal power or storage.
Systems using mechanical/electrical power (pumps, fans, tracking) to collect/move solar heat or run collectors.
Building design that collects, stores, and distributes solar heat without (or with minimal) active machinery.
CF = energy produced over a period ÷ (nameplate capacity × hours in period).
RE resource that can be captured with available technology and practical constraints (less than theoretical; more than economic in many framings).

sections.title: RE definition and the SEE trilemma

blocks.text: Renewables displace fossil fuel combustion — cutting I via T in IPAT and supporting SDG 7. Policy must still keep lights on and bills fair.

items: Security: reliability, diversity, resilience of supply.
Equity: access, affordability, just transition.
Environment: low local pollution and low GHG intensity.

blocks.text: SEE = Security, Equity, Environment. Name all three; one-sided optimization fails the trilemma.
Links Week 2 SDGs and Week 4 mitigation; Week 6 extends to geothermal, ocean, hydro, bio.

blocks.use: Kinetic power in airflow through rotor swept area A; ρ air density; v wind speed.
Betz: maximum fraction of wind power extractable by an ideal actuator disk.
Because (1/2)×(16/27) = 8/27 — memorize this compact form.

blocks.title: v³ scaling intuition
rows: Small speed gains matter a lot

blocks.text: Drill: P ∝ v³; Betz 16/27; P_max = (8/27)ρAv³. Site selection cares more about wind resource than blade area alone.
Applying Betz Cp to P_max formula twice (double-counting) is a common error. Use either Cp×½ρAv³ or 8/27 form once.

sections.title: Solar: PV vs CSP; active vs passive

blocks.title: Active vs passive solar
rows: Solar water heater with circulating pump

blocks.text: Trombe wall: south-facing (N hemisphere) glazed gap + massive dark wall. Day: sun heats wall; night: heat conducts/convects indoors. Classic passive exam example.
Match Trombe → passive. CSP ≠ PV. Diffuse-cloud climates favour PV over CSP.

blocks.use: Dimensionless (or %); wind/solar CF << 1 because resource is variable.

items: Theoretical potential: physical upper bound of the resource.
Technical potential: after technology, siting, and system constraints.
Economic potential: what clears cost thresholds.
Market/sustainable potential: further policy and sustainability filters.

blocks.text: Capacity factor ≠ efficiency. CF is utilization of nameplate over time; Betz Cp is aerodynamic efficiency bound.
Example pattern: 2 MW turbine, 8760 h/y, CF=0.35 → annual energy ≈ 2×8760×0.35 MWh.
Equating technical potential to ‘what is installed today’ understates resource; equating it to theoretical overstates deployable RE.

Solar PV: tilt, azimuth, temperature derating, soiling.

definitions.definition: Enhanced Geothermal System: engineered reservoir — stimulate fractures in hot rock, circulate water/brine, extract heat where natural hydrothermal flow is inadequate.

Higher tidal range when Sun, Moon, and Earth are aligned (new/full moon).

blocks.text: Conventional hydrothermal uses naturally permeable hot reservoirs. EGS expands the map to hot dry rock by creating heat-exchange pathways.

blocks.use: Heat extraction rate: mass flow × specific heat × temperature drop (wellhead vs reinjection/datum).

sections.title: Ocean energy: OTEC, wave, tidal ranking

blocks.text: OTEC cycles: closed (working fluid, e.g. ammonia), open (seawater flash → steam → condenser), hybrid. Needs large ΔT (tropical surface vs deep cold).
Memorize order and numbers: OTEC 44000 ≫ wave 29500 ≫ tidal 1200 TWh/y.
Largest theoretical ≠ easiest to deploy. Tidal sites are localized; OTEC is tech-hard despite huge potential.

Tidal barrage/ lagoon: exploit potential energy of tidal range. Tidal stream: kinetic power when currents ≳ 1.5–2 m/s. Average power depends on range, basin area, or stream speed distribution over the lunar cycle.

items: Spring tides: Sun–Moon–Earth aligned → larger range → more energy.

blocks.text: Wave energy ∝ H² — height measurement errors dominate. Spring vs neap definition is a free MCQ.

blocks.use: Potential energy of mass m raised/lowered through head z.

blocks.text: Hydraulic power ≈ ρ Q g z with Q volumetric flow. Large dams store energy; run-of-river has less storage. Head and flow dominate — free-stream kinetic of a river is usually secondary behind a dam.

weeks.title: Industrial Ecology and Circular Economy
atAGlance: Urban metabolism = anabolism (build stocks) + catabolism (wastes/emissions).
Linear slogan: Take-Make-Waste. Circular slogan: Borrow-Use-Return.
CE principles: eliminate waste/pollution; circulate at highest value; regenerate nature.
CE elements: closed cycles + renewable energy + systems thinking.
9R ladder R0-R9: tighter (lower-R) loop = more circular.
Exam order among subset: Recycle < Repurpose < Repair < Rethink.
Five circular business models; nesting IS subset of IE subset of CE; Kalundborg and Kujala.

definitions.definition: Sum of technical and socioeconomic processes in a city that produce growth, energy use, and waste elimination — matter and energy flows through the urban system.
definitions.trap: Not only waste management; includes inflows, stocks, and outflows.

definitions.definition: Processes that build and maintain urban stocks (buildings, infrastructure, products).
definitions.trap: Do not swap with catabolism.

definitions.definition: Processes that break down stocks and generate wastes, emissions, and heat leaving the city.
definitions.trap: Do not swap with anabolism.

definitions.definition: One-way Take-Make-Waste throughput that depletes natural capital and runs down the parent ecosystem.
definitions.trap: An efficient linear plant is still linear, not circular.

definitions.definition: Keep products and materials at highest utility via reuse, repair, remanufacture, recycle; minimize virgin inputs and waste; regenerate natural systems.
definitions.trap: Recycling alone is not a circular economy.

definitions.definition: Preferred hierarchical circular strategies from Refuse (R0) to Recover (R9). Tighter loops need fewer external inputs.
definitions.trap: Order matters more than listing names.

definitions.definition: Say no to unnecessary, single-use, or non-recyclable items so they never enter the system.
definitions.trap: Refuse is not the same as Reduce.

definitions.definition: Redesign product, service, or ownership so waste is avoided (e.g. shared printers instead of one per desk).
definitions.trap: Not just think green; it is redesign of delivery or ownership.

definitions.definition: Use less dangerous, wasteful, or non-recyclable product so waste and resource demand fall (source reduction).
definitions.trap: Source reduction is not recycling.

definitions.definition: Use again with little or no reprocessing (refill bottle, donate clothes).
definitions.trap: Melting plastic into new pellets is recycle, not reuse.

definitions.definition: Restore performance and postpone replacement; preserves embodied value.
definitions.trap: Preserves more value than recycle.

definitions.definition: Life-extend a component into a second life cycle; role may change.
definitions.trap: Not the same as remanufacture.

definitions.definition: Industrial rebuild to like-new or better-than-new condition, typically with warranty; keeps more embodied energy than material recycle.
definitions.trap: Remanufacture is not simple repair.

definitions.definition: Give discarded product or material a new function (e.g. turbine blades used as structures).
definitions.trap: Goal is to slow virgin throughput.

definitions.definition: Convert waste into new materials or objects; lower on the circularity ladder than repair or reuse.
definitions.trap: Less circular than repair, reuse, or rethink.

definitions.definition: Recover resources or energy so less material goes to final disposal; lowest R preference before dump.
definitions.trap: Energy recovery is not preferred over material loops.

definitions.definition: Study and design of industrial systems that mimic ecosystems: material and energy cycling and controlled exchanges with nature. Scales from park to city to nation to globe.
definitions.trap: IE is broader than one eco-park case.

definitions.definition: Firms share resources so one plant's by-product, waste, energy, or water becomes another's feedstock.
definitions.trap: IS is a subset of IE, not a synonym for all of CE.

definitions.definition: Biological and technical cycles that keep materials circulating at highest value (Ellen MacArthur framing).
definitions.trap: Repair and reuse sit above shred-to-recycle.

blocks.text: Society depends on natural resources. Cities act like organisms: they take in materials and energy, build stocks, and expel wastes. Mapping inflows and outflows shows whether the urban system is sustainable.

items: Anabolism: build and maintain urban stocks (buildings, roads, goods).
Catabolism: generate wastes, emissions, and heat that leave the city.
Urban metabolism = anabolism + catabolism as matter and energy accounting.
Over-exploitation of resources stresses ecosystems that supply the city.

blocks.title: Linear vs circular urban economy
rows: Aims to keep natural capital intact

blocks.text: Closing loops cuts virgin extraction, landfill, and emissions, and opens new business models. Benefits span environmental, social, and economic dimensions.
Memorize exact slogans: Take-Make-Waste vs Borrow-Use-Return. Also anabolism = build stocks; catabolism = wastes/emissions.

sections.title: CE principles, elements, and SDG link

blocks.text: Circular economy redesigns production and consumption so materials stay in use. It is a pathway toward sustainability, not a synonym for sustainability itself.

items: Eliminate waste and pollution by design.
Circulate products and materials at their highest value.
Regenerate natural systems.
Element 1 — Closed cycles: keep materials looping (reuse to remanufacture to recycle).
Element 2 — Renewable energy: power loops without fossil lock-in.
Element 3 — Systems thinking: design across firms, cities, and supply chains.

blocks.text: CE strongly supports SDG 12 (Responsible Consumption and Production). Sustainability is the broader 3-pillar goal; CE is one operational route.
High recycling rates alone do not prove circularity if consumption still grows and losses remain (e.g. even high Al can recycling leaves virgin demand if use expands).
The 9Rs define preferred strategies. Rule: tighter loop (lower R number) = more circular; longer loop = less preferred. Always state order, not a random list.

blocks.title: Full 9R ladder with examples
rows: Shared office printers instead of one per desk
Fix a phone screen; right-to-repair parts
Restore used laptop for resale as second life
Rebuild electric motor to like-new with warranty
Wind turbine blades reused as park structures
Melt PET bottles into new polymer feedstock
Incinerate residual waste with energy recovery

blocks.text: Assignment ordering pattern among a subset: Recycle < Repurpose < Repair < Rethink (least to most circular). Value retention: repair keeps more embodied value than shredding for recycle (Butterfly logic).
Remanufacture CO2 numerical (course example): new motor emits about 5.0 t CO2; remanufacture about 1.5 t CO2. Saving per motor = 3.5 t. For 65 motors: 3.5 x 65 = 227.5 t CO2 avoided.

blocks.expr: CO2 saved = (CO2_new - CO2_reman) x N = 3.5 t/motor x 65 = 227.5 t
blocks.use: Compare remanufacture vs new production for embodied GHG; exam numerical.

blocks.text: Reuse is not recycle. Melting plastic is R8 Recycle. Rethink means redesign of product/service/ownership — not just repairing what exists.
Firms operationalize 9R ideas through business model choice. Match each model to its defining trait and a named example.

blocks.title: Five circular business models
rows: AkzoNobel steam from waste incineration; AeroFarms local food
Lease / pay-per-use; provider owns risk and end-of-life
Patagonia repair / Don't buy this jacket
Closed-loop by-product or waste to feedstock
Take-back and recycle into new product (Timberland-style)

blocks.text: MCQs often give a vignette (lease engine hours; shared printers; take-back shoes) — map vignette to one of the five models.

Industrial ecology designs industry like ecosystems: materials and energy cycle; exchanges with nature (extraction and emissions) are managed. Industrial symbiosis is network-level by-product exchange among firms.

blocks.use: Nesting assertion: industrial symbiosis inside industrial ecology inside circular economy.

items: By-product synergies: waste of A becomes feedstock of B.
Utility / infrastructure synergies: shared steam, water, energy grids.
Knowledge synergies: joint learning and process design.

blocks.title: Flagship cases

items: Example flows: waste heat to greenhouses; tyre shavings to construction; fish-farm sludge to fertilizer.
Exam assertion: symbiosis raises cluster efficiency because waste becomes feedstock.

blocks.text: Name Kalundborg and Kujala. Define IS as firm-to-firm resource sharing. State nesting IS ⊂ IE ⊂ CE.
CE is necessary but not automatically sufficient. Exams often ask for at least two limitations.

items: Thermodynamics: every cycle still consumes resources and emits wastes; perfect closure is impossible.
System boundaries: spatial problem-shifting along the life cycle; temporal trade-offs.
Physical scale and rebound (boomerang) effect: efficiency can raise total consumption.
Path-dependency and lock-in of early technologies and infrastructure.
Governance: hard to manage inter-organization and inter-sector material flows.
High recycling alone fails if consumption grows and residual losses remain.

blocks.text: Do not claim CE abolishes the laws of thermodynamics. Always pair CE praise with at least one hard limit.

weeks.title: Water Quality, Reuse and Recycling
atAGlance: Global water: ~97.5% salt / ~2.5% fresh; usable freshwater is tiny.
Withdrawal is not consumption (consumption = water not returned).
India BOD often BOD3 at 27 C; COD is usually greater than or equal to BOD.
NBOD approx NH3-N x 4.57; DO sag then recovery via reaeration.
NSF-WQI: DO weight 0.17 (highest); fecal coliform 0.16.
CPCB BOD3 maxima: inland 30 / sewers 350 / irrigation 100 mg/L.
NGT Act date 18.10.2010; endeavor dispose in 6 months; 5 seats.
Tertiary treatment needed for food-crop / unrestricted recreation reuse.

definitions.definition: Water extracted from surface or groundwater sources.
definitions.trap: Not the same as consumption.

definitions.definition: Withdrawn water not returned to the source (evaporation, incorporation in product, transpired).
definitions.trap: Drinking and cooking are consumptive uses.

definitions.definition: Identifiable discrete outlet such as a pipe or drain.
definitions.trap: Urban stormwater runoff is typically non-point.

definitions.definition: Microbial oxygen demand to stabilize biodegradable organics. In India often reported as BOD3 at 27 C.
definitions.trap: Not always BOD5 at 20 C (US/standard lab convention).

definitions.definition: Oxygen demand measured with a strong chemical oxidant; usually greater than or equal to BOD.
definitions.trap: High theoretical O2 demand can still mean low BOD if organics are hard to biodegrade.

definitions.definition: Dissolved oxygen drops after an organic load, then recovers as reaeration catches up.
definitions.trap: Before the critical point, deoxygenation exceeds reaeration.

definitions.definition: Aggregated water-quality score from weighted sub-index values of selected parameters.
definitions.trap: Band is not a single-parameter reading.

definitions.definition: Specialized National Green Tribunal under the 2010 Act; natural justice; expert plus judicial members.
definitions.trap: Also heavily tested in Week 12.

blocks.text: Most Earth water is saline. Freshwater is scarce and unevenly distributed. Off-stream uses withdraw water; instream uses leave water in the channel. Environmental flows must remain for ecosystems.

items: About 97.5% of global water is salt water; about 2.5% is fresh.
Of freshwater, groundwater is a large share (~30.1%); surface freshwater is a tiny slice (~0.3% of freshwater).
Municipal wastewater is often ~80% of urban water use; Indian cities cited ~87%.
Household design figure often ~100 L per capita per day in course notes.

blocks.text: 97.5% salt / 2.5% fresh is a staple MCQ. Always separate withdrawal from consumption.
Point sources have a clear outlet. Non-point sources are diffuse (agriculture, urban runoff). Quality is judged with physical, chemical, and biological parameters.

items: Physical / chemical: SS, pH, temperature, oil and grease, residual chlorine.
Nitrogen species: NH3-N, TKN; also phosphorus for eutrophication.
Oxygen demand: BOD, COD; pathogens via fecal coliform.
DO is both a quality parameter and the driver of sag curves.

blocks.text: Primary clarification removes settleable solids; it is not the main BOD-removal step. Secondary biological treatment targets BOD.
Oxygen demand links organics to DO depletion. COD is a chemical upper bound; BOD is the biodegradable share. Nitrogenous BOD follows carbonaceous BOD in time.

blocks.use: Estimate nitrogenous oxygen demand from ammonia nitrogen concentration.

items: India standard for many discharge limits: BOD3 at 27 C.
COD is typically greater than or equal to BOD.
Hardness often expressed as CaCO3 equivalent.
TS / VS solids lab data also appear in bioprocess suitability (shared with W9).

blocks.text: Memorize factor 4.57 for NBOD. Memorize BOD3 @ 27 C as the India convention.
After a wastewater mix, DO falls as microbes oxidize organics, then rises as reaeration restores oxygen. The lowest DO is the critical point at critical time tc.

blocks.use: Oxygen deficit definition used in sag analysis.

items: Mix effluent with river (mass balance on BOD and DO).
Deoxygenation rate exceeds reaeration → deficit grows.
At critical point, rates balance; DO is minimum.
Downstream, reaeration dominates → recovery.
Nitrification sequence: Org-N → NH3 → NO2 (Nitrosomonas) → NO3 (Nitrobacter).
Nitrification adds a second oxygen demand pulse (NBOD).

blocks.text: Qualitative DO sag rules are frequently tested even when full Streeter-Phelps algebra is not.
WQI compresses many parameters into one score. Horton (1965) and NSF (1970 Delphi) weights are classic. Weighted Qi values are summed.

blocks.use: Compute NSF-style index from sub-index Qi and weight Wi.

blocks.text: DO weight 0.17 is the single most tested NSF number. Know band cut-points.
Discharge limits depend on destination. Reuse for food crops or unrestricted recreation needs tertiary polishing. ZLD is an aspiration for some industrial clusters.

Principal bench New Delhi; other benches Bhopal, Pune, Kolkata, Chennai.
Natural justice; endeavor to dispose cases in 6 months.
Not bound by CPC 1908 procedure (detailed again in W12).

definitions.definition: Waste that is not free-flowing liquid or gas; containerized liquid or gas wastes can still be counted as solid waste under rules.
definitions.trap: Do not assume only dry solids count.

definitions.definition: Integrated Solid Waste Management: coordinated policies and technologies from generation through disposal.
definitions.trap: Not a single technology fix.

definitions.definition: Prevent > Reuse > Recycle > Recover > Dispose — preference order for managing waste.
definitions.trap: Landfill is last even if engineered.

definitions.definition: Fraction of total solids lost on ignition; proxy for organic content.
definitions.trap: VS% of wet mass is not the same as VS% of TS.

definitions.definition: Engineered disposal with cells, daily cover, liners, leachate collection, and landfill-gas control.
definitions.trap: Not the same as an open dump.

definitions.definition: Thermal breakdown of organics in the complete absence of air.
definitions.trap: Not incineration (with air) and not gasification (limited air/oxygen).

definitions.definition: Biological treatment without oxygen that produces biogas.
definitions.trap: Not composting (which is aerobic).

definitions.definition: Extended Producer Responsibility: producer remains responsible for end-of-life collection and recycling.
definitions.trap: Course frames clear EPR first in E-waste Rules 2011.

definitions.definition: Recover metals and rare earth elements from discarded electronics.
definitions.trap: India lacks rich natural REE deposits — urban mining matters.

blocks.text: Integrated SWM coordinates generation, collection, processing, and disposal. Preference always starts with prevention and source reduction.

items: Prevent — avoid creating waste (green design).
Reuse — use product again.
Recycle — remake materials.
Recover — energy or material recovery from residual.
Dispose — sanitary landfill as last resort.
4Rs: Reduce, Reuse, Recycle, Recover.
EcoMark: BIS environmental label; symbol is an earthen pot.

blocks.text: PRRRD order and 4Rs are first-line MCQs. EcoMark earthen pot is a classic trick question.

MSW generation rises with income. Paper fraction rises with income; Indian MSW remains organic-rich. Hazardous traces matter even at low mass fraction.

items: Average C/N of Indian MSW about 33.4 (composting suitability marker).

blocks.text: Fe is not one of the toxic five. If an option list sneaks in iron, reject it.
Source segregation decides whether organics, recyclables, and toxics can be treated separately. Collection logistics dominate municipal budgets.

items: Collection often consumes 50-70% of the MSW management budget.
Mixed collection contaminates recyclables and organics.
Transfer stations and route design cut haul costs.

blocks.text: 50-70% budget share for collection is a high-yield number.

blocks.expr: TS = 100% - moisture%; VS (% of TS) = (mass lost on ignition / TS mass) x 100%
blocks.use: Convert wet-basis moisture to TS and then to organic fraction of solids.

blocks.text: Worked pattern: 40% moisture means TS = 60%. If 50 of those 60 units are lost on ignition, VS = 50/60 = 83.3% of TS.
Always check whether VS is reported on wet mass or on TS basis before comparing numbers.
Options include recycling, composting, anaerobic digestion, incineration, gasification, pyrolysis, and sanitary landfill. Open dumping is unacceptable.

weeks.title: Noise Pollution
atAGlance: Noise = unwanted sound with physiological, psychological, or interference effects.
Lp = 20 log10(Prms / 20 uPa); 0 dB corresponds to 20 uPa.
Wavelength lambda = c/f; speed c approx 20.05 sqrt(T) with T in kelvin.
Point source: about -6 dB per distance doubling; line source: about -3 dB.
Two equal incoherent sources: +3 dB; if levels differ by >=10 dB, total ~ louder source.
A-weighting mimics human ear; preferred for environmental and occupational limits.
Occupational caution: >=85 dB(A) for 8 h.

blocks.text: River Ib Barrage rapid EIA shows why alternatives analysis matters. Objectives included irrigating about 800 ha and supplying drinking/industrial water to Jharsuguda, Brajrajnagar, and Belpahar.

Conclusion: barrage alone is inadequate; EIA must condition or reject before build.
